summary: When Pharisees accuse His hungry disciples of breaking the Sabbath in a grainfield, Jesus answers from Scripture and declares Himself Lord of the Sabbath.
key_insight: Jesus answers the charge three times from Scripture, and each answer reaches higher: David’s need, the temple’s service, and finally Himself. The question was about grain; the answer is about who Jesus is.
story: One Sabbath Jesus was walking through the grainfields with His disciples. They were hungry, {Mt} and as they went they began to pluck heads of grain, rub them in their hands {Lk} and eat.
Some of the Pharisees saw it and said to Jesus, “Look, Your disciples are doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath!” {Mt}

Jesus answered, “Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, he and those who were with him?” In the days of Abiathar the high priest, {Mk} David went into the house of God and ate the showbread, which only the priests were allowed to eat, and gave some to the men with him.

Then Jesus pointed to the Law itself. Every Sabbath the priests in the temple work, and they are blameless. “Yet I say to you that in this place there is One greater than the temple.” If the Pharisees had known what “I desire mercy and not sacrifice” means, they would not have condemned the guiltless. {Mt}
He added, “The Sabbath was made for man, and not man for the Sabbath.” {Mk} And He ended with a claim about Himself: “The Son of Man is also Lord of the Sabbath.”
differences: Only Matthew says the disciples were hungry. Only Luke says they rubbed the grain in their hands, and he dates the day “the second Sabbath after the first.”
In Matthew and Mark the Pharisees speak to Jesus about the disciples; in Luke they question the disciples directly, and Jesus answers.
Only Mark says David’s meal happened “in the days of Abiathar the high priest,” and only Mark records “The Sabbath was made for man, and not man for the Sabbath.”
Matthew alone adds the priests who work in the temple on the Sabbath, “One greater than the temple,” and Hosea’s “I desire mercy and not sacrifice.”

fit.question: Mark says David ate the showbread “in the days of Abiathar the high priest.” But 1 Samuel 21 says the priest who gave him the bread was Ahimelech, Abiathar’s father. Did Mark get the name wrong?

points.label: The passage about Abiathar
points.text: Mark’s Greek phrase can point to the section of Scripture about Abiathar, a way of finding a passage in the scroll before chapters and verses existed. Mark uses the same kind of phrase in 12:26, which the NKJV renders “in the burning bush passage.”

points.label: In Abiathar’s time
points.text: Abiathar was a priest at Nob, Ahimelech’s son. He alone escaped when Saul later killed the priests there, fled to David (1 Samuel 22:20–23) and served as his high priest for decades (1 Kings 2:26–27). “In the days of” can mark the era of the better-known man.

points.label: Names shared in one family
points.text: The Old Testament itself reverses the names: 2 Samuel 8:17 and 1 Chronicles 24:6 speak of “Ahimelech the son of Abiathar.” Father and son may both have been known by both names.

fit.note: This is one of the harder questions in the Gospels. Careful scholars give more than one good answer, and none of them requires that Mark erred.
fit.short: Mark may point to the Scripture passage about Abiathar, or to the time of Abiathar, Ahimelech’s son, who soon became David’s high priest.

scene.label: Plucking grain
scene.text: The Law let a hungry traveler pluck heads of grain from a neighbor’s field by hand (Deuteronomy 23:25). The Pharisees did not call it stealing. Their tradition counted plucking as reaping and rubbing as threshing, two kinds of work forbidden on the Sabbath.

scene.label: The showbread
scene.text: Twelve loaves were set before the Lord in the holy place every Sabbath, and the old loaves were eaten by the priests alone (Leviticus 24:5–9). When David fled from Saul, the priest at Nob gave him the old loaves because there was no other bread (1 Samuel 21:1–6).

scene.label: Priests at work
scene.text: The Sabbath brought extra work in the temple. Priests changed the showbread and offered extra burnt offerings (Numbers 28:9–10). The Law itself required this work, and no one called it sin.

scene.label: “The second Sabbath after the first”
scene.text: Luke’s phrase appears nowhere else, and its meaning is uncertain; some of the oldest manuscripts omit it and say only that it was a Sabbath. Many think it counts Sabbaths from Passover. Ripe grain in the fields fits the spring harvest season, which began around Passover.

witnesses.matthew: Gives the fullest defense. He alone adds the priests in the temple, the claim that “One greater than the temple” is here, and Hosea 6:6, which Jesus had already quoted at the dinner after Matthew’s call (Matthew 9:13). In Matthew, the King is greater than the temple and reads the Law with God’s own heart of mercy.
witnesses.mark: Alone keeps the saying that the Sabbath was made for man, God’s gift of rest rather than a burden laid on people. Mark sets this dispute right beside the healing in the synagogue (3:1–6), so two Sabbath conflicts lead straight to the plot to destroy Jesus.
witnesses.luke: Dates the event to “the second Sabbath after the first” and notes the disciples rubbing the grain in their hands, the detail that made it threshing in the Pharisees’ eyes. In Luke the Pharisees challenge the disciples, and Jesus steps in to answer for them.

seeing.reveals: Jesus sets Himself above the temple and calls Himself Lord of the Sabbath. He does not throw the Sabbath away; He claims the right to say what it is for.
seeing.living: The Pharisees knew the rules and missed the mercy of God standing in the field with them. Receive God’s rest as a gift from its Lord, and when you are quick to condemn others over religious practice, remember Hosea: God desires mercy.
seeing.ponder: Where have you been quicker to condemn the guiltless than to show the mercy God desires?

preaching.big_idea: The One greater than the temple is Lord of the Sabbath, and He desires mercy.
outline: An answer from the heart of God (7–8)
preaching.watch_for: Each answer begins by asking what the Pharisees had not read or not known (vv. 3, 5, 7). Men who prided themselves on the Scriptures are sent back to them three times.
